newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak declines comment c.bank decision.
newsitem.headline: Slovak declines comment c.bank decision.

text.p: Slovak steelmaker VSZ a.s. on Thursday declined to comment on the central bank's rejection of its bid to increase its holdings in commercial bank IRB a.s.
"It is necessary to take certain steps and decisions ...and then I will talk about it, maybe in a few weeks, time, but not now," VSZ President Jan Smerek told Reuters.
The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) on Wednesday said it had rejected a request made by VSZ in August to increase its holdings in IRB, the third largest commercial bank, to over 20 percent.
VSZ's holdings in IRB caused a stir recently when it was revealed that it might have exceeded 15 percent, which by law needs central bank approval.

Shortly after the request was filed, the Central Securities Registry (SCP) published figures showing VSZ already held some 20 percent of IRB, but later retracted the figures without further explanation.

Before the NBS decision was announced, Smerek had said VSZ was interested in increasing its stake in IRB to as much as 40 percent. But on Thursday he declined to specify how large a stake VSZ now hoped to gain in IRB.

"We hope most to gain synergic effects in our activities in the banking sphere because the amount of money and actual trade within the VSZ group is big enough to help us save money on transactions and be profitable," Smerek said.
VSZ is a major client of IRB, accounting for an estimated 1.5 percent of the bank's total loan portfolio.
Smerek added that there were ways for VSZ to attain its goals even if did not have the central bank's blessing. He did not elaborate.

He rejected allegations that VSZ could bring IRB to bankruptcy by spreading its activities through its 100-odd subsidiaries. "Why should we allow IRB to become bankrupt? We have not considered any such thing," he said.
IRB is on a government list of strategic companies as well as being part of a group of banks that will undergo loan portfolio restructuring.
The state holds a 35 percent stake in IRB through its privatisation agency the National Property Fund (NPF).
